section.title: The Limits of Wisdom
section.sectionRationale: After the gloom of chapter six, the Teacher turns to a string of proverbs, but with a sober edge. He prefers the house of mourning to the house of feasting, praises the rebuke of the wise over the song of fools, and then presses into the hardest ground: the righteous who perish and the wicked who thrive, the danger of both excess, and his own confession that wisdom, though good, remained beyond his reach. The chapter honors wisdom and, in the same breath, marks its limits.
section.thesis: Wisdom is a real and life preserving good, better than folly and better than empty pleasure, yet it cannot straighten what God has bent, cannot fathom the deep scheme of things, and cannot make anyone righteous; the crookedness of the world and the sinfulness of every heart drive us beyond human wisdom to the fear of God.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the wisdom of sorrow, mourning better than feasting and rebuke better than the song of fools; wisdom as a shelter under the crooked work of God; the middle path and the fear of God amid the righteous who perish and the wicked who thrive; and the Teacher's search that reaches its limit, no one righteous, and mankind bent on many schemes.

verses.text: A good name is better than fine perfume, and one’s day of death is better than his day of birth.
It is better to enter a house of mourning than a house of feasting, since death is the end of every man, and the living should take this to heart.
Sorrow is better than laughter, for a sad countenance is good for the heart.
The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, but the heart of {{kesil|fools}} is in the house of pleasure.
It is better to heed a wise man’s rebuke than to listen to the song of fools.
For like the crackling of thorns under the pot, so is the laughter of the fool. This too is {{hevel|futile}}.

units.label: Wisdom as a shelter under God's crooked work
units.note: who can straighten what He has bent

verses.text: Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool, and a bribe corrupts the heart.
The end of a matter is better than the beginning, and a patient spirit is better than a proud one.
Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool.
Do not say, “Why were the old days better than these?” For it is unwise of you to ask about this.
{{chokmah|Wisdom}}, like an inheritance, is good, and it benefits those who see the sun.
For wisdom, like money, is a shelter, and the advantage of knowledge is that wisdom preserves the life of its owner.
Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?
In the day of prosperity, be joyful, but in the day of adversity, consider this: God has made one of these along with the other, so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him.

units.label: The middle path and the fear of God
units.note: the righteous perish, the wicked thrive

verses.text: In my {{hevel|futile}} life I have seen both of these: A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness.
Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise. Why should you destroy yourself?
Do not be excessively wicked, and do not be a fool. Why should you die before your time?
It is good to grasp the one and not let the other slip from your hand. For he who fears God will follow both warnings.
Wisdom makes the wise man stronger than ten rulers in a city.
Surely there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins.

units.label: The search that reaches its limit

verses.text: Do not pay attention to every word that is spoken, or you may hear your servant cursing you.
For you know in your heart that many times you yourself have cursed others.
All this I tested by wisdom, saying, “I resolve to be wise.” But it was beyond me.
What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?
I directed my mind to understand, to explore, to search out wisdom and explanations, and to understand the stupidity of wickedness and the folly of madness.
And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is a net, and whose hands are chains. The man who pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is ensnared.
“Behold,” says the Teacher, “I have discovered this by adding one thing to another to find an explanation.
While my soul was still searching but not finding, among a thousand I have found one upright man, but among all these I have not found one such woman.
Only this have I found: I have discovered that God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes.”

hevel.gloss: Vapor, breath, mist, the refrain of Ecclesiastes translated 'futile.' It names life as fleeting and hard to grasp. Even the laughter of the fool is hevel, a quick crackle of thorns; even the Teacher's own days are called his 'futile life,' brief and slippery as breath.

chokmah.gloss: Wisdom, the skill of living well and rightly before God and others. In this chapter wisdom is genuinely praised, a shelter like money, a strength greater than ten rulers, life preserving, and yet the Teacher confesses it 'was beyond me': real wisdom knows its own limits and bows to the fear of God.

kesil.gloss: Fool, not the simply ignorant but the one who despises wisdom and lives for shallow pleasure. The fool's heart is in the house of mirth, his laughter a brief crackle of burning thorns; the Teacher sets him against the wise, whose heart is willing to sit in the house of mourning and learn.

basic.context: The Teacher gathers a set of proverbs that run against our instincts. A good name matters more than luxury, and the day of death teaches more than the day of birth. It is better, he says, to sit in a house of mourning than a house of feasting, because grief makes us wise and death is where we all end. He praises wisdom as a real shelter, yet insists it has hard limits: no one can straighten what God has bent, no one can see the future, and the world is full of righteous people who suffer and wicked people who prosper. He warns against self righteous extremes, calls us to fear God, and finally admits that full wisdom was beyond even him. His last word is blunt: God made people upright, but we have all gone chasing our own schemes.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter honors wisdom and marks its boundaries at the same time. The proverbs are not gloomy for its own sake; they are sober realism that makes the heart wise. The key confessions are that wisdom cannot straighten God's crooked providence, 7:13, cannot fathom the deep scheme of things, 7:24, and cannot produce a righteous person, since 'there is no righteous man who does good and never sins,' 7:20. Read rightly, the chapter does not despair of wisdom; it drives us past our own wisdom to the fear of God and, ultimately, to the wisdom of God found in Christ.
basic.originalLanguages: Three words shape the chapter. Chokmah, wisdom, is genuinely praised, a shelter and a strength, yet the Teacher says it 'was beyond me.' The kesil, the fool, lives for shallow mirth, his laughter a quick crackle of thorns. And hevel, breath or vapor, still hums underneath: the fool's laughter is 'futile,' and the Teacher calls his own days his 'futile life,' fleeting and hard to hold.
basic.typology: The confession that no one is righteous and never sins, 7:20, anticipates Paul's verdict that all have sinned, and points to the need for a righteousness from God. The truth that no one can straighten what God has bent points ahead to Christ, in whom the crookedness of the world is finally set right. The deep scheme of things 'out of reach' is opened in Him, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom.
basic.christ: Human wisdom in this chapter runs into a wall: it cannot straighten the world, cannot fathom its depths, and cannot make anyone righteous. Every one of those limits is answered in Christ. He is the wisdom of God, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. He is the righteousness we lack, for 'there is no one righteous,' and God makes us righteous in Him. And He is the one who was made subject to the world's futility in order to set the crooked straight, so that what no wise man could bend back, God bends back through the cross and resurrection.
basic.god: God stands behind both the prosperity and the adversity, 7:14, and no one can undo His work or predict His future. He is the one to be feared, and that fear is the path between self righteous extremes. He made mankind upright; the crookedness is ours, not His. This God is not the problem to be solved but the refuge to be trusted where wisdom runs out.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3 declares that no one is righteous, echoing 7:20. 1 Corinthians 1 and Colossians 2 present Christ as the wisdom of God in whom all treasures of wisdom are hidden. Proverbs 9 says the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Romans 8 speaks of creation subjected to futility in hope.
basic.oneStory: Wisdom is good, but it cannot straighten the crooked world or cleanse the crooked heart. The Teacher pushes human wisdom to its honest edge and leaves us fearing God and needing more than we can find under the sun. The Bible answers with Christ, the wisdom and righteousness of God, who straightens what we cannot and gives what we could never search out.

context.literary:
Chapter 7 changes the form of the book. Up to this point the Teacher has mostly told stories of his own experiments, 'I said in my heart', 'I turned', 'I saw'. Here he gathers sayings, and the first of them are in the classic Hebrew pattern 'better than'. A good name is better than fine perfume, the end of a matter is better than its beginning, patience is better than pride. The first saying carries a pun, since the Hebrew for 'name' and for 'perfume' (shem and shemen) are nearly the same sound. The run is a lesson in the Proverbs style, and it is meant to be remembered.

The chapter has four movements, but they do not follow one another smoothly. Verses 1 to 6 praise the house of mourning. Verses 7 to 14 describe wisdom as a shelter and then break against the line 'Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?' Verses 15 to 22 are the notorious middle, with warnings about being overly righteous and overly wise, held together by a confession that no one is righteous. Verses 23 to 29 then bring the Teacher back into the first person for the last time in the chapter, as he describes his search for wisdom and what it found.

A number of word links hold the movements together. The 'thorns under the pot' of verse 6 are in Hebrew a wordplay of sirim and sir, and in verse 12 wisdom and money are each a 'shelter', literally a shadow, the same word that described a life that passes 'like a shadow' at the end of chapter 6. The crooked and the straight of verse 13 look back to 1:15, 'What is crooked cannot be straightened', and the anger that settles in the lap of the fool in verse 9 is the same Hebrew word as the 'sorrow' that is better than laughter in verse 3. Perhaps most important, the search for 'explanations' in verses 25 and 27 is answered by the 'schemes' of verse 29, and the Hebrew word is from the same root. The Teacher went looking for the reckoning of the world and found the reckonings that humans have devised.
context.historical:
The chapter takes the form of the sage's school. In Israel and in her neighbours, wisdom was handed down in short sayings that trained young people to read their world. The house of mourning mattered because mourning was a public event: a household sat with the bereaved for days, and the young who attended learned what the old already knew. Feasting, in turn, was the other side of a social life organised around meals, weddings and harvest. When the Teacher says it is better to go to the house of mourning, he is recommending an education.

The courtly background is visible in verse 7. 'Extortion' and 'a bribe' are the mechanisms by which a wise official could be corrupted, and verse 19, 'ten rulers in a city', recalls the councils of a town, where one wise person could be worth more than the whole board. A reader who takes the book as coming from Solomon's court will think of the tradition that credits him with 'three thousand proverbs', 1 Kings 4:32. A reader who places it later will hear the voice of a teacher in an imperial setting. Either way, it is the language of someone who had seen powerful people at work.

The woman of verses 26 to 28 has to be read in this setting. Proverbs warns the young man again and again about a woman whose house is the way to the grave, Proverbs 7:27, and about a woman whose ways lead down to death, and her counterpart is Folly, who calls from the high places of the city, Proverbs 9:13 to 18. A king with many wives would have particular cause for the remark, and the tradition remembers that Solomon's wives 'turned his heart', 1 Kings 11:3. The Teacher is a man writing from the experience of the court, and it is the court's snare that he names.

The moral claim in the last verse reaches behind all of this, to the beginning. 'God made mankind upright' is a statement of Genesis 1:31, that the world and the people in it were very good when He made them.
context.canonical:
The chapter's central confession, 'there is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins', has older roots. Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple says 'there is no one who does not sin', 1 Kings 8:46, and Proverbs asks 'Who can say, "I have kept my heart pure; I am cleansed from my sin"?', Proverbs 20:9. The psalmist says that 'no one alive is righteous before You', Psalm 143:2. Paul takes up exactly this line in Romans 3:10 to 12, 'There is no one righteous, not even one', and builds his case for justification by faith on it. Ecclesiastes 7:20 is therefore a link in a chain that runs from the temple through the Psalms to Romans.

Wisdom's limits connect with Job and with Proverbs. Job is the book of a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, which is the first half of Ecclesiastes 7:15, and its closing chapters teach him that God's work cannot be fathomed by the sage. The Teacher's confession in verse 24, 'What exists is out of reach and very deep', is Job's 'things too wonderful for me', Job 42:3. Proverbs says the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge, Proverbs 1:7, and the Teacher's 'he who fears God will follow both warnings', 7:18, takes that for its anchor.

The New Testament picks up two themes. The first is that the crooked will be straightened. The people of God had hoped for a road made smooth, Isaiah 40:4, and Luke applies that promise to the ministry that announces Christ: 'The crooked ways shall be made straight', Luke 3:5. The second is that Christ is the wisdom that the Teacher could not find. Paul calls Him 'wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption', 1 Corinthians 1:30, and says that in Him 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge', Colossians 2:3. And the last verse, God made mankind upright but they sought out schemes, is the Bible's whole account of Genesis 3 compressed in a sentence.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Teacher wants his hearers to learn from the places they would rather avoid. The first six verses are an argument against taking the easy road, which is to measure a good life by how often one laughs. He wants the reader to go and sit where there is grief, and to leave with a heart that has been taught something that a feast cannot teach. He is not recommending misery. He is recommending the honesty that comes from remembering that every life ends.

He wants his hearers to hold wisdom as a real good and to hold it humbly. Wisdom is a shelter, but it is a shelter and not a god, and it cannot straighten what God has bent. That is the point of verse 13, and a person who has absorbed it will neither fall into despair when the world does not make sense nor become the kind of person who thinks his cleverness can fix the world. The advice about the middle path in verses 16 to 18 serves the same purpose: it is a protection against both a brittle self righteousness and a careless slide into wickedness.

The last section is a confession that is meant to be shared. The Teacher says he resolved to be wise and discovered that it was beyond him. A reader who has been trusting his own insight is meant to hear that and stop. And in the final line, he states the one thing he could find, that God made people upright and they have sought out schemes. That sentence is his answer to anyone who blames God for the crooked world, and his invitation to anyone who thinks the crookedness is only out there. The reader is meant to turn from the world to the heart, and from the heart to the fear of God.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the chapter is wisdom advice, and some of it is plain command, such as 'Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit', verse 9, and 'Do not say, "Why were the old days better than these?"', verse 10. Those can be taken as direct instruction. The statements about God's work in verses 13 and 14 are descriptions of how the world is, and a reader should not turn them into a command to do nothing about crookedness. The Bible elsewhere calls us to act justly, to pray and to work for good, and the Teacher's point is only that the final straightening is God's.

The hardest verses to apply are 16 and 17, and verses 26 to 28 on the woman. The warning not to be 'overly righteous' is not a licence to sin a little, and it does not cancel the call to be holy, since the same chapter insists on fearing God and on the universal reality of sin. It is a warning against a self made righteousness that exalts itself and ends up being destructive. The comments about women in verses 26 to 28 are a report of the Teacher's own search and a warning against a kind of snare, not a principle about the worth of women. The narrator's own last line, in verse 29, puts the blame on 'mankind', and not on one sex.

What carries forward most clearly is the humility. Whatever the proverb, the lesson is that a person should accept the limits of his wisdom, receive prosperity and adversity as coming from God, and live in the fear of the LORD.

debates.question: What does 'Do not be overly righteous, and do not make yourself too wise' mean in verses 16 to 18?

views.label: A call to moderation, a golden mean
views.case: Many read verses 16 and 17 as advice to avoid extremes in both directions, too much religion and too little, and take 'he who fears God will follow both warnings' as the Teacher's endorsement of a balanced life. The BSB footnote notes the Hebrew can be taken as 'will avoid all extremes'.

views.label: A rebuke to self righteousness
views.case: The warning is aimed at the person who thinks he is righteous enough to be safe, who is 'overly righteous' in his own eyes. The very next sentence says there is no righteous man who never sins, verse 20, which undermines any pretence of excess righteousness. On this reading the target is the legalist and the proud sage, and the 'wicked' warning in verse 17 sets the opposite fault beside it.

views.label: An observation about the unfairness of life
views.case: The verses follow a statement that a righteous man can perish in his righteousness, verse 15. Some take 16 and 17 as the Teacher's sober counsel not to stake your life on the hope that your goodness will protect you, nor to give up on goodness altogether. It is realism, not a rule.

debates.bearing: The text does not endorse moderate sin, and the book ends with the command to fear God and keep His commandments, 12:13. The second reading best fits the Teacher's own conclusion in verse 20, and the third explains the context, while the first is correct in the sense that the chapter wants a balanced life. What the chapter means to produce is the humble fear of God that avoids both errors.

debates.question: How should the woman of verses 26 to 28 be understood?

views.label: The adulteress or seductress, as in Proverbs
views.case: The snare and net imagery recalls Proverbs 7:23 to 27, where the seductress is a trap that leads to death. The line that the man who pleases God escapes her and the sinner is caught matches that teaching. This reading takes it as a warning to young men, from a man who knew the snare of the court.

views.label: Lady Folly, a personification
views.case: Proverbs presents Wisdom and Folly as two women calling from the city, Proverbs 9. On this reading the Teacher speaks of Folly, who ensnares the sinner, while the one who pleases God escapes her. The 'one man in a thousand, no woman' would then be about the rarity of true wisdom.

views.label: A bitter personal finding, bounded by verse 29
views.case: The Teacher says, 'I have found', and he marks it as his own search. Verse 29 then turns to the universal verdict, which is that God made mankind upright and all have sought schemes. On this view the Teacher is reporting what he found in his own experience, and the last verse corrects any reading that blames one sex. The Hebrew uses a feminine form for the Teacher's own verb in verse 27, which some take as a sign that the book's voice is not narrowly male.

debates.bearing: The passage must be read within the Teacher's own conclusion in verse 29, which puts the universal fault in mankind. The first reading has the most support from Proverbs, and the second shows that the figure may be larger than any one woman. In either case, the text does not teach that women are worse than men. It warns against a specific snare and then states that all people, men and women, have gone astray.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is the Hebrew for 'sorrow' in verse 3. It is ka'as, a word that elsewhere is usually rendered 'anger' or 'vexation'. It appears again in verse 9, where the BSB has 'provoked' and 'anger', and the two uses are bound together: 'Do not be quickly provoked in your spirit, for anger settles in the lap of a fool.' So the saying that ka'as is better than laughter may be about the useful sting of vexation, the sort of grief that sets a heart straight, and the same word in verse 9 warns against the sort that rules it. The BSB footnote at verse 9 notes the Hebrew says 'in the bosom of fools', so anger is pictured as something that is held and nursed.

The second is the pair 'crooked' and 'straighten' in verse 13. The Hebrew for 'bent' is the word that in 1:15 describes what is crooked and cannot be straightened. The Teacher repeats the point with God as the subject: 'Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?' The verb for 'straighten' is also the one used at the end of the book, 12:9, of the Teacher himself, who 'arranged many proverbs'. The man can set proverbs in order, but he cannot set the world in order.

The third is the 'one who fears God' in verse 18, and the verb that follows. The BSB says he 'will follow both warnings', but the Hebrew idiom is to 'go out' with both, and so the line can be rendered as the BSB footnote says, 'will avoid all extremes', or as 'will come through both'. The sense is that the person who fears God is not caught in the dilemma that the Teacher has just described.

The fourth is the word for 'explanations' and 'schemes'. In verses 25 and 27 the Teacher wants to find the reckoning, cheshbon, of things, and in verse 29 humans have sought out 'schemes', chishvonot. They share a root that has to do with calculating and devising. The Teacher went to the world looking for the account of how things add up, and found only the accounts that people have invented for themselves. Thinking of it this way, verse 29 is not a separate point but the finding of the search.

The fifth is the pair of words in verse 24, 'out of reach' and 'very deep', where the Hebrew doubles the word for deep, 'deep, deep', a way of saying very deep indeed. It matches Job's meditation on the places of wisdom, Job 28:12 to 14, where the deep says 'It is not in me'.

The sixth is 'ten rulers' in verse 19. The word for 'rulers' belongs to the same family as the verbs for authority that the Teacher uses in 5:19 and 8:4. Wisdom gives more strength than the combined authority of a council, which is a way of saying that insight gives a kind of power that office cannot.

typology.type: The crooked that no one can straighten, 7:13
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher says that what God has bent no one can straighten. Isaiah promises a levelled road for the Lord, Isaiah 40:4, and Luke applies it to the ministry that announces Christ: 'The crooked ways shall be made straight', Luke 3:4 to 5. In Christ, the One who bent is also the One who sets right: He heals, forgives and, at the end, makes all things new, Revelation 21:5. Paul says the creation was subjected to futility 'in hope', Romans 8:20, which is the straightening that the Teacher could only long for. The type is still unfolding, since the full straightening awaits the new creation.

typology.type: The righteous man who perishes in his righteousness, 7:15
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher notes that a righteous man can die while the wicked live long. Jesus is the one case in which this reaches its limit: the only truly righteous One was put to death, and 'He had done no violence, nor was any deceit in His mouth', Isaiah 53:9. Peter says that He 'suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God', 1 Peter 3:18. The correspondence is that a righteous man perished. The escalation is that this perishing was for others, and God raised Him, which resolves what the Teacher sees as unresolved.

The Teacher's diagnosis, that no one does good and never sins, is the ground of Romans 3:10 to 12, where Paul quotes the Psalms to say there is no one righteous. The answer is that a righteousness comes from God by faith in Jesus Christ, Romans 3:21 to 22, and that Christ 'has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption', 1 Corinthians 1:30. The pattern is a need and its answer. The type falls short because the Teacher knows the need without having the supply.

typology.type: Wisdom out of reach and very deep, 7:23 to 24
typology.fulfillment: The Teacher says that wisdom was beyond him. Paul says of Christ that 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge', Colossians 2:3, and Proverbs gives wisdom a voice that calls from the heights, Proverbs 8:1 to 4. What no sage could fathom is given in a person. The correspondence is that the search ends in a person, and Paul adds the praise of Romans 11:33, 'the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God'. The type falls short because the full knowledge of God will await the day we see Him face to face, 1 Corinthians 13:12.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ by its three failures of human wisdom, and each has an answer in Him. The first is the crooked world. 'Who can straighten what He has bent?' The Gospel says that God has acted: the One who bent the world in judgment has entered it, and in Christ He is bringing it back. Paul describes the creation as subjected to futility 'in hope that the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to decay', Romans 8:20 to 21. The Teacher's question about who can straighten is answered by the One on the throne who says, 'Behold, I make all things new', Revelation 21:5. The cross itself is the great bending, the righteous One put to death, and the resurrection is the straightening.

The second is the righteousness no one has. Verse 20 is the Teacher's most direct anticipation of the gospel. 'There is no righteous man on earth who does good and never sins', and Paul quotes the thought in Romans 3:10 to 12 to show that every mouth is silenced. The answer is not a call for more effort. The Teacher's warning against excessive righteousness would have been cruel if righteousness could be reached by trying harder. The gospel says that a righteousness has been given, because God made the One who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God, 2 Corinthians 5:21. And so Christ becomes 'wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption', 1 Corinthians 1:30. Righteousness and wisdom come together in Him, as they could not in a sage.

The third is the wisdom no one can reach. 'I resolve to be wise', the Teacher says, 'but it was beyond me.' The New Testament says that the wisdom has come near. Jesus is called the wisdom of God, 1 Corinthians 1:24, and in Him 'are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge', Colossians 2:3. He says of Himself, 'I am the way and the truth and the life', John 14:6. The Teacher searched and did not find; the Lord said, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened', Matthew 11:28, and they who come to Him find. In Matthew 12:42 Jesus even says of Himself that 'One greater than Solomon is here', which fits a book whose voice is that of the son of David.

There is also the pattern of the sorrowful. The Teacher says that the heart of the wise is in the house of mourning, and Jesus is called 'a man of sorrows', Isaiah 53:3, who wept at the grave of a friend, John 11:35, and who said 'Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted', Matthew 5:4. The chapter's praise of sorrow is realised in Him, because He went into the house of mourning, and carried grief, and turned it into comfort. The fear of God that the Teacher recommends is found perfectly in Him, who 'delights in the fear of the LORD', Isaiah 11:3. A caution is needed. Not every detail, such as the woman of verse 26, is to be turned into a portrait of Christ, and the links above are those that the New Testament makes itself.
study.god:
The chapter's picture of God is of One who works in ways that human wisdom can neither alter nor predict. 'Consider the work of God: Who can straighten what He has bent?' The Teacher does not say the world is out of God's hands. On the contrary, he says that in the day of prosperity and the day of adversity, 'God has made one of these along with the other', verse 14. Good days and hard days both come under His making. That is a demanding teaching, and it is held with the other things the chapter says: that God made mankind upright, and that the crookedness is ours. The tension is not resolved by the Teacher. He holds God's sovereignty over all things and mankind's responsibility for sin together, and so does the Bible as a whole.

The chapter also teaches that God is the end of the search. 'What exists is out of reach and very deep. Who can fathom it?' The Teacher's repeated failure to reach the bottom of things is not meant to produce cynicism. It is the Bible's way of saying that God is greater than our categories. Job's closing confession, 'Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know', Job 42:3, is the proper end of the road the Teacher is walking, and Paul's doxology is its cheerful form: 'O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!', Romans 11:33.

God is also the one who can be feared. The fear of God in verse 18 is not terror but the right posture of a creature before a Creator, which is the beginning of knowledge, Proverbs 1:7. It is the thing that lets a person move between a rigid righteousness and a careless wickedness without falling into either. The fear is practical because it keeps the person honest about himself: it does not let him claim a righteousness he does not have, or write off the obligations he does.

Finally, the chapter shows God as the one who made people good. 'God made mankind upright' stands against every attempt to say that the Creator is the cause of our crookedness. This is the claim of Genesis 1:31, that all God made was very good, and it matters for worship because it means we may thank Him for creation and trust His character even when we cannot understand His work. It also sets the ground for grace. If humanity were made crooked, there would be nothing to restore. Because it was made upright, the God who made it can set it right.

In worship, then, the chapter calls for a mixture of sorrow and gratitude. We sit in the house of mourning to remember our mortality, and we thank the God who made us for a better thing than what we have made of ourselves. In prayer, it teaches us to ask for wisdom, as James urges, and to do so in the knowledge that He gives generously, James 1:5.

crossReferences.note: The Teacher says at the start of the book that what is crooked cannot be straightened. Chapter 7:13 repeats it with God as the agent, 'Who can straighten what He has bent?' It shows that the crookedness of the world is not an accident but part of what the Teacher found about the work of God.

In his prayer at the dedication of the temple, Solomon says there is no one who does not sin. Ecclesiastes 7:20 states the same truth from the sage's point of view. Both give a reason why a sanctuary of sacrifice and forgiveness had to be built.

The proverb asks who can say they have kept their heart pure and are cleansed from their sin. It is the question form of Ecclesiastes 7:20, and the answer expected in both is that no one can. The Teacher gives a statement, and the proverb a challenge.

Paul quotes the Psalms to say that there is no one righteous, not even one, and builds his argument for justification by faith on it. Ecclesiastes 7:20 is an Old Testament statement of the same fact, which Paul extends to show that all stand in need of God's gift.

Job concludes that he spoke of things too wonderful for him to know. It is the end of the same road the Teacher is walking in Ecclesiastes 7:23 to 24, where wisdom is far off and very deep, and it shows the fitting response to a world that exceeds our grasp.

Paul says that creation was subjected to futility in hope of being set free from bondage to decay. It gives the New Testament's answer to the Teacher's question about who can straighten what God has bent: God Himself, in Christ, in the end.

Christ has become for us wisdom from God, our righteousness, holiness and redemption. Wisdom and righteousness, which the Teacher found out of reach and impossible to produce in Ecclesiastes 7:20 and 7:23, are given together in a single person.

In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. It answers the Teacher's statement that wisdom was beyond him and very deep, Ecclesiastes 7:23 to 24, by saying that the treasure house has been opened in a person.

God looked on all He had made and called it very good. Ecclesiastes 7:29 returns to this, saying God made mankind upright, and it identifies the fall as the source of the schemes that have followed. The Teacher's last discovery is in fact the first chapter of the Bible.

After the fall the pair sewed fig leaves to cover themselves. It is the first human scheme, a device invented to deal with shame, and it is the pattern of the many schemes of Ecclesiastes 7:29, where mankind keeps devising its own solutions.

The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge. The Teacher says that he who fears God will follow both warnings, Ecclesiastes 7:18, and the proverb gives the reason: fear is where wisdom starts, and what the Teacher could not reach by search comes from there.

The psalmist asks God not to bring His servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before Him. It uses the same confession as Ecclesiastes 7:20, but as the ground of a prayer for mercy, which is where the Teacher's observation leads.

study.oneStory:
Ecclesiastes 7 gathers up the whole story from creation to the cross in a handful of verses. The last verse is the best summary of Genesis 1 to 3 in the Old Testament outside Genesis. God made mankind upright, which is the 'very good' of Genesis 1:31. They sought out schemes, which is the fig leaves, the hiding and the blaming of Genesis 3. Between those two statements lies everything that the Teacher has found: a crooked world, a sinful heart, and a wisdom that cannot reach either.

The crookedness he cannot straighten is the consequence of the fall, described in Genesis 3:17 to 19, and Paul explains in Romans 8:20 that creation itself was subjected to futility. The righteousness he cannot find is the thing that Adam had and lost, and the rest of the Old Testament is the story of God's attempt to make a people who could be righteous: the law, the sacrifices, the prophets, the kings. Every one of them, in its way, showed that there was no one who does good and never sins. The temple prayer of 1 Kings 8:46 and the psalms of confession belong to the same movement.

The wisdom he cannot reach is the wisdom that was also in the beginning. Proverbs 8 describes Wisdom as present at creation, and the New Testament takes this up in Christ, 'through whom He made the universe', Hebrews 1:2, and in whom the treasures of wisdom are hidden. The long search of the Old Testament sages is a search for the person who is there at the end. The Teacher can say only that it was beyond him. Paul says that Christ crucified is 'the power of God and the wisdom of God', 1 Corinthians 1:24.

The chapter's prayer for a righteous man who does not perish is also answered in the course of the story. The one righteous Man did perish, and rose, so that a world of unrighteous people could be made righteous. And its longing for the crooked to be straightened is met when the whole creation is renewed. In the last chapters of the Bible the curse is gone, the tree of life is back, and God's people see His face, Revelation 22:3 to 4. There the schemes cease, since the heart is made new, and mankind is again as God made it, upright, living in the fear and the joy of the Lord.

quiz.q: Why does the Teacher prefer the house of mourning to the house of feasting, 7:1-4?

options.text: Because facing death makes the heart wise, while the fool's mirth avoids reality.
options.note: The funeral teaches what the party cannot; the living take it to heart.

options.text: Because sorrow is always better than any kind of laughter.
options.note: Close to verse 3, but the deeper point is that mourning makes us wise, not that joy is bad.

options.text: Because feasting is sinful and forbidden.
options.note: The Teacher elsewhere commends eating and drinking with joy; he is not banning feasts.

options.text: Because the wise never feel any gladness.
options.note: The book repeatedly commends real joy; this is sober wisdom, not joylessness.

quiz.q: What does 7:13 mean by 'Who can straighten what He has bent?'

options.text: God orders the world, including its crookedness, and human wisdom cannot undo His work.
options.note: It confesses the limit of wisdom before God's inscrutable providence.

options.text: People should try harder to fix the world's problems.
options.note: The verse says the opposite: what God has bent, no one can straighten by effort.

options.text: God will always make crooked things straight immediately.
options.note: It rightly senses God is at work, but the point is present inability to straighten it, not a promise of instant repair.

options.text: Wisdom can solve any problem if applied correctly.
options.note: The verse marks exactly the boundary of wisdom before God's work.

quiz.q: What does 7:20 declare about human righteousness?

options.text: There is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins.
options.note: A universal statement of human sinfulness, echoed in Romans 3.

options.text: Most people are righteous, with only a few exceptions.
options.note: It rightly admits sin is widespread, but the verse is universal: no one does good and never sins.

options.text: Only the wicked sin; the wise are sinless.
options.note: The Teacher includes everyone, wise and foolish alike.

options.text: Righteousness is impossible to define.
options.note: The verse is not about defining righteousness but about universal sin.

quiz.q: How should 'Do not be overly righteous', 7:16, be understood?

options.text: As a warning against self made, presumptuous righteousness that judges God's ways, resolved by fearing God.
options.note: Held with 7:20 and 7:29, it exposes the limits of self righteousness, not a call to mediocrity.

options.text: As counsel to avoid extremes and fear God on the middle path.
options.note: The fear of God is central, though the sharper point is the danger of self destroying presumption.

options.text: As permission to sin a little as long as not too much.
options.note: Verse 17 also warns against wickedness and folly; this is not a license to sin.

options.text: As advice to aim for comfortable moral mediocrity.
options.note: The Teacher targets presumption, not the pursuit of genuine godliness.

quiz.q: How do the limits of wisdom in this chapter point to Christ?

options.text: Wisdom cannot straighten the world, fathom its depths, or make us righteous, all of which are answered in Christ, the wisdom and righteousness of God.
options.note: Colossians 2:3 and 1 Corinthians 1:30 present Christ as the answer to these very limits.

options.text: It shows that wisdom is valuable, as Christ also taught.
options.note: True, but it underplays how directly Christ answers the specific limits named here.

options.text: It teaches that we should abandon wisdom entirely.
options.note: The chapter praises wisdom even while marking its limits; it does not discard it.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ.
options.note: Its confession of sin and of wisdom's limits runs straight to Christ, the wisdom of God.

questions: The Teacher says the funeral teaches more than the feast. What has a season of grief or loss taught you that comfort never could?
Wisdom, he admits, cannot straighten what God has bent. Where are you exhausting yourself trying to fix or control something you may need to entrust to God instead?
Verse 20 says no one does good and never sins, and that includes you and me. How does honestly owning your own sin change the way you judge others, or the way you come to God?
The chapter warns against a self made righteousness that presumes to master life. Where might you be leaning on your own goodness or cleverness rather than on the fear of God?

The deep things stayed 'out of reach' for the Teacher, yet Christ is the wisdom of God in whom all treasures of wisdom are hidden. What would it look like to bring a question you cannot answer to Him this week?

translationNotes.note: 'Futile' renders hevel, breath or vapor; the image is a fool's laughter as the quick crackle of burning thorns under a pot, loud, bright, and gone in a moment.
'He who fears God will follow both warnings' can also be rendered 'will avoid all extremes.' The fear of God is the anchor that steers between presumptuous righteousness and reckless folly.
The verse states human sinfulness in universal terms; Paul draws on it in Romans 3 to show that all have sinned and need the righteousness God gives in Christ.
'God made mankind upright, but they have sought out many schemes' locates the crookedness in human hearts, not in God, echoing the fall and setting up the need for redemption.
